Part A · Unit 1

Semiconductor physics

Every device in this course is made of doped silicon. This part answers three things: what carries current in silicon, how many carriers there are, and what makes them move. Parts B to E reuse all three.

ConstantValueConstantValue
Electron charge q1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ CThermal voltage VT = kT/q≈ 26 mV at 300 K (25.9 mV)
Boltzmann constant k1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV/KBand gap EgSi 1.12 eV · Ge 0.67 eV · GaAs 1.42 eV
Si atoms per cm³5 × 10²²ni of Si at 300 K≈ 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ (slides) · 1.5 × 10¹⁰ in many books
Unit 1 › Materials

A1 · Energy bands, electrons and holes

Practice · built on slides 19–24 of the Unit 1 deck Using energy bands, explain why heating lowers the resistance of a semiconductor but raises the resistance of a metal.
Guess first, on paper.
Valence electron: an outer electron that forms bonds. Si has 4. · Covalent bond: two neighbouring atoms share a pair of valence electrons. · eV: the energy one electron gains crossing 1 volt, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

Bands. In a crystal the allowed electron energies form bands. The valence band holds the electrons locked in bonds. The conduction band holds electrons that are free to move. Between them is the band gap Eg, where no states exist.

Electron–hole pairs. At 0 K every Si bond is full and silicon is an insulator. At room temperature, heat breaks a few bonds. Each broken bond gives one free electron (in the conduction band) and leaves one hole, a missing electron that behaves as a mobile charge of +q. Pure silicon therefore always has equal numbers: n = p = ni, the intrinsic concentration.

Size of ni. About 10¹⁰ per cm³ in Si at 300 K, against 5 × 10²² atoms per cm³, so only one bond in 10¹² is broken. ni rises steeply with temperature: ni² ∝ T³·e−Eg/kT. In Si it roughly doubles every 10 °C (slide 37). A smaller gap means a larger ni, so Ge (0.67 eV) is leakier than Si (1.12 eV).

Answer. Semiconductor: heating breaks more bonds, so the number of carriers rises exponentially. That outweighs the extra scattering, so resistance falls (negative temperature coefficient). Metal: the bands overlap, so the number of free electrons is fixed. Heat only makes the atoms vibrate more, which scatters the electrons more, so resistance rises (positive temperature coefficient).
Check A1. (a) What are the two carriers in a semiconductor, and what is each physically? (b) Why is n = p in pure silicon? (c) Which has the larger ni at 300 K, Si or Ge, and why?
Unit 1 › Materials

A2 · Doping and the mass-action law

Practice · numbers follow the slides' ni = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ Silicon is doped with ND = 10¹⁶ donor atoms per cm³. At 300 K, find the electron and hole concentrations.
Guess first: will there be more holes or fewer holes than in pure silicon?
Doping: adding a tiny, controlled amount of another element. · Donor: an atom with 5 valence electrons (P, As, Sb); the fifth is given away as a free electron. · Acceptor: an atom with 3 valence electrons (B, Al, Ga); the missing bond is a hole.

Extrinsic silicon. Doped silicon is called extrinsic. Donors make it n-type: electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority. Acceptors make it p-type, with the roles swapped. At room temperature every dopant atom is ionised, so

n-type: n ≈ ND   ·   p-type: p ≈ NA

Mass-action law. In equilibrium the product of the two concentrations is fixed by temperature alone, doped or not:

n · p = ni²

Adding electrons makes holes rarer, because a hole now meets an electron and recombines sooner. Charge neutrality still holds: the crystal is neutral because each free electron left behind a fixed positive donor ion (n + NA = p + ND). If both dopants are present, the larger one wins: n ≈ ND − NA (a compensated semiconductor).

Answer. n ≈ ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³. p = ni²/n = (10¹⁰)²/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³. Holes dropped from 10¹⁰ to 10⁴. With ni = 1.5 × 10¹⁰ the same steps give p = 2.25 × 10⁴ cm⁻³.
Check A2. (a) Silicon has NA = 5 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ of boron. Name its type and find p and n (ni = 10¹⁰). (b) A doped bar has billions of extra free electrons. Why is it still electrically neutral?
Unit 1 › Carrier statistics

A3 · The Fermi level

Practice · derivation on slide 38 of the Unit 1 deck Show that the Fermi level of an intrinsic semiconductor lies at the middle of the forbidden gap.
Guess first: which way does EF move when donors are added?
State: a slot an electron may occupy at a given energy. · f(E): the probability that a state at energy E is occupied. · NC, NV: effective number of states at the conduction-band and valence-band edges.

Fermi–Dirac function. Electrons fill states from the bottom up. The probability that a state at energy E is filled is

f(E) = 1 / (1 + e(E − EF)/kT)

EF, the Fermi level, is the energy where f = ½. Well above EF states are almost empty; well below, almost full. Counting the filled conduction-band states and the empty valence-band states gives

n = NC e−(EC − EF)/kT     p = NV e−(EF − EV)/kT

So EF is a gauge. Close to EC means many electrons (n-type). Close to EV means many holes (p-type). For n-type material, EF − Ei = kT ln(ND/ni), where Ei is the intrinsic (mid-gap) level. At very high temperature ni catches up with the doping and EF drifts back to mid-gap.

Answer. Intrinsic means n = p: NC e−(EC − EF)/kT = NV e−(EF − EV)/kT. Take NC = NV. Then the exponents are equal: EC − EF = EF − EV, so EF = (EC + EV)/2. Without that assumption an extra term appears, EF = (EC + EV)/2 + (kT/2) ln(NV/NC), which is only a few meV.
Check A3. (a) What is f(EF) at 300 K and at 600 K? (b) For ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and ni = 10¹⁰, how far is EF above mid-gap? (c) Find f(E) for a state 0.1 eV above EF at 300 K.
Unit 1 › Carrier transport

A4 · Drift, mobility, conductivity, sheet resistance

Professor's Unit 1 deck · slide 51 · Example (a) Calculate the conductivity and resistivity of intrinsic silicon at T = 300 K. (b) How would σ change if the temperature increases by 10 °C? Given: μn = 1500 cm²/V-s, μp = 450 cm²/V-s at 300 K.
Guess first: bigger or smaller than 1 Ω·cm?
Electric field E: volts per cm; the force per unit charge. · Current density J: current per unit cross-section area, A/cm². · Scattering: a carrier colliding with a vibrating atom or an ion and losing its direction.

Drift. A field accelerates carriers, and scattering keeps stopping them, so they settle at an average drift velocity vd = μE. Mobility μ (cm²/V·s) measures how easily a carrier moves. Electrons are faster than holes (Si: μn ≈ 1350–1500, μp ≈ 450–480). Mobility falls when temperature or doping rises, because both add scattering. At very high fields vd stops rising (velocity saturation, about 10⁷ cm/s in Si).

Both carriers add to the current, since holes move with the field and electrons against it but carry opposite charge:

Jdrift = q(nμn + pμp)E = σE     σ = q(nμn + pμp)     ρ = 1/σ

Answer. (a) n = p = ni = 10¹⁰. σ = q ni(μn + μp) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁰ × 1950 = 3.12 × 10⁻⁶ (Ω·cm)⁻¹, so ρ = 1/σ = 3.2 × 10⁵ Ω·cm. (b) ni doubles for a 10 °C rise while the mobilities barely change, so σ doubles. Slide 52 then dopes the same silicon with ND = 5 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³: σ = 32 (Ω·cm)⁻¹, ten million times larger. One donor per 10⁵ atoms does that.

Sheet resistance. IC resistors are thin doped layers of fixed thickness t. Group ρ/t into one number, the sheet resistance Rs = ρ/t, in ohms per square (Ω/□). Then R = Rs × L/W. A square of any size has resistance Rs; a strip 10 squares long has 10 Rs.

Check A4. n-type Si has ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and μn = 1350 cm²/V·s. Find (a) σ and ρ, (b) the drift velocity in a field of 100 V/cm, (c) the sheet resistance of a layer 1 μm thick, (d) the resistance of a strip with L/W = 10.
Unit 1 › Carrier transport

A5 · Diffusion, the Einstein relation, total current

Practice In a silicon bar the electron concentration falls by 10¹⁸ cm⁻³ over every cm of length. Take μn = 1350 cm²/V·s at 300 K. Find the diffusion coefficient and the electron diffusion current density.
Guess first: no voltage is applied. Can a current still flow?

Diffusion. Carriers move randomly because of heat. If one side is more crowded, more carriers wander out of it than into it, so there is a net flow from high concentration to low. No field is needed. The flow is proportional to the slope of the concentration (the gradient, dn/dx), and the constant is the diffusion coefficient D (cm²/s):

Jn,diff = +qDn dn/dx     Jp,diff = −qDp dp/dx

The signs differ because electrons carry −q: electrons moving in +x make a current in −x.

Einstein relation. Drift and diffusion are both limited by the same scattering, so D and μ are tied together:

Dn/μn = Dp/μp = kT/q = VT ≈ 26 mV at 300 K

Total current. Each carrier can drift and diffuse at once:

Jn = qnμnE + qDn dn/dx     Jp = qpμpE − qDp dp/dx     J = Jn + Jp

In equilibrium Jn = 0 and Jp = 0 separately: wherever a gradient exists, a built-in field sets up a drift that cancels the diffusion exactly. That balance is what happens inside a pn junction (Part B).

Answer. Dn = μnVT = 1350 × 0.0259 = 34.9 cm²/s. |J| = qDn|dn/dx| = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 34.9 × 10¹⁸ = 5.59 A/cm². Electrons flow toward the emptier end; the current points the other way.
Check A5. (a) Find Dp for μp = 480 cm²/V·s at 300 K. (b) Name the cause of drift current and the cause of diffusion current in one phrase each. (c) Write the total hole current density.
Unit 1 › Carrier dynamics

A6 · Generation, recombination, continuity and Poisson equations

Practice · syllabus line "Generation and recombination of carriers; Poisson and continuity equation" Write the continuity equation for electrons and state what each term means.
Guess first: list every way the number of electrons in a small box can change.

Generation (G) creates an electron–hole pair: heat or light lifts an electron across the gap. Recombination (R) destroys a pair: an electron drops into a hole. In equilibrium G = R, which is what holds n·p at ni². Direct (band-to-band) recombination releases light and dominates in GaAs, which is why LEDs use it. In Si and Ge the electron usually drops in two steps through a trap, an impurity or defect level near mid-gap (indirect, or Shockley–Read–Hall, recombination), and the energy becomes heat.

Lifetime τ. Extra (excess) minority carriers Δp do not vanish at once. They recombine at a rate Δp/τ, so they decay as Δp(t) = Δp(0)e−t/τ. τ is the minority-carrier lifetime. It sets how fast a diode can switch off (B3).

Continuity equation. It is bookkeeping for a thin slice of material: carriers inside change only because more flow in than out, or because of net recombination.

∂n/∂t = (1/q) ∂Jn/∂x − (R − G)      ∂p/∂t = −(1/q) ∂Jp/∂x − (R − G)

Poisson equation. It links charge to field: wherever there is net charge, the field changes with position.

dE/dx = ρ/ε = (q/ε)(p − n + ND − NA)     and     E = −dV/dx

ρ here is charge density (C/cm³) and ε the permittivity of silicon (11.7 ε0). In neutral material ρ = 0 and the field is constant. In a depletion region ρ ≠ 0, so the field ramps. B1 uses exactly this.

Answer. ∂n/∂t = (1/q) ∂Jn/∂x − (R − G). Left side: the rate of change of electron concentration at a point. First term: the net flow of electrons into the slice (current in minus current out). Second term: the net loss by recombination over generation. For holes the flow term changes sign because the charge is +q.
Check A6. (a) Why does recombination in silicon mostly go through traps? (b) Excess holes have τ = 1 μs. What fraction is left after 3 μs? (c) In which region of a device is the charge density ρ not zero?

Answers: Part A Checks

  1. A1. (a) Free electrons in the conduction band, and holes: missing bond electrons in the valence band that act as +q charges. (b) Each broken bond makes exactly one of each. (c) Ge. Its gap is smaller (0.67 eV against 1.12 eV), so heat breaks more bonds.
  2. A2. (a) p-type. p ≈ 5 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³, n = 10²⁰/(5 × 10¹⁷) = 200 cm⁻³. (b) Every free electron left behind a fixed donor ion of charge +q.
  3. A3. (a) ½ at both. (b) kT ln(10¹⁶/10¹⁰) = 0.0259 × 13.8 = 0.357 eV. (c) 1/(1 + e0.1/0.0259) = 1/(1 + 47.7) ≈ 0.0205, about 2%.
  4. A4. (a) σ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁶ × 1350 = 2.16 (Ω·cm)⁻¹; ρ = 0.462 Ω·cm. (b) vd = μE = 1.35 × 10⁵ cm/s. (c) Rs = ρ/t = 0.462/10⁻⁴ cm = 4620 Ω/□. (d) R = 10 × 4620 = 46.2 kΩ.
  5. A5. (a) Dp = 480 × 0.0259 = 12.4 cm²/s. (b) Drift: an electric field. Diffusion: a concentration gradient. (c) Jp = qpμpE − qDp dp/dx.
  6. A6. (a) Si has an indirect gap, so a direct drop is unlikely; a mid-gap trap lets the electron fall in two easy steps. (b) e⁻³ ≈ 0.05, so 5%. (c) The depletion (space-charge) region.
Part B · Unit 2

The PN junction and diode circuits

Put p-type and n-type silicon in contact and you get a one-way valve for current: the diode. B1–B3 explain the device. B4–B8 are the circuits, where most of the numerical marks are. B9 covers the special diodes from the slides.

Unit 2 › The junction

B1 · Junction formation, depletion region, built-in voltage

Professor's Unit 1–2 deck · slides 77–78 · Examples For an abrupt silicon pn junction, the built-in voltage is Vbi = 0.85 V. Let W0 and W1 denote the depletion widths for Va = 0 V and Va = 0.6 V, respectively. What is W1/W0? Repeat for a reverse bias of 2 V.
Guess first: does forward bias make the depletion region wider or narrower?
Abrupt junction: the doping switches from p to n in one step. · Ion: a dopant atom that has lost its carrier; it is charged but fixed in the crystal. · Bias: a DC voltage applied across the device.

Formation. At the moment of contact, holes diffuse from p to n and electrons from n to p (A5), and they recombine. They leave behind fixed ions: negative acceptor ions on the p side, positive donor ions on the n side. This strip with no free carriers is the depletion region (or space-charge region). The ions create a field pointing from n to p that pushes carriers back. Diffusion stops when this drift exactly cancels it. The voltage across the region at that balance is the built-in voltage:

Vbi = VT ln(NAND / ni²)

Vbi is about 0.6–0.9 V in Si. A voltmeter reads zero across an unconnected diode, because the metal contacts add equal and opposite steps.

Width. Solving Poisson's equation (A6) in the depletion region gives a triangular field and

W = √[ (2ε/q)(1/NA + 1/ND)(Vbi − Va) ]     NAxp = NDxn

Va is the applied voltage, positive for forward bias. The region reaches further into the lightly doped side, since both sides must hold equal charge.

Bias. Forward bias (p positive) lowers the barrier to Vbi − Va: the region narrows and majority carriers pour across. Reverse bias (p negative) raises the barrier: the region widens and only a tiny current of thermally generated minority carriers flows.

Answer. W ∝ √(Vbi − Va). Forward 0.6 V: W1/W0 = √(0.25/0.85) = 0.54, the region shrinks. Reverse 2 V (Va = −2): W2/W0 = √(2.85/0.85) = 1.83, it expands.
Check B1. (a) Find Vbi for NA = 10¹⁷, ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, ni = 10¹⁰, VT = 25.9 mV. (b) In that junction, which side holds more of the depletion region? (c) What two currents balance at equilibrium?
Unit 2 › The junction

B2 · The diode I–V characteristic

Practice · equation from slides 79–83 A diode has Is = 1 pA and η = 1 at 300 K. Find its current at VD = 0.6 V. What happens to the current if VD rises by 60 mV?
Guess first.

Shockley equation. Lowering the barrier lets exponentially more carriers cross, so

ID = Is(eVD/ηVT − 1)     VT = kT/q = T/11600 ≈ 26 mV at 300 K

SymbolMeaning
IsReverse saturation current. The small current of minority carriers in reverse bias: nA for Si, μA for Ge. Proportional to ni².
ηIdeality factor, between 1 and 2. The slides use η = 1 for Ge and 2 for Si. Take η = 1 unless told otherwise.
Knee (cut-in) voltageWhere the current becomes noticeable: about 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge, 1.2 V for GaAs.

Three regions. Forward (VD ≫ VT): the −1 is negligible and ID ≈ IseVD/ηVT. Reverse: the exponential dies and ID ≈ −Is, flat. Breakdown: at a large reverse voltage the current rises sharply (B8).

Temperature. Is about doubles for every 10 °C rise: Is2 = Is1 · 2(T₂ − T₁)/10 (slide 81). At a fixed current the forward voltage falls about 2 mV per °C, so the whole forward curve shifts left when the diode heats up.

Answer. ID = 10⁻¹² × (e0.6/0.0259 − 1) = 10⁻¹² × 1.2 × 10¹⁰ = 12 mA. Adding 60 mV multiplies the current by e0.06/0.0259 ≈ 10. Every 60 mV is a factor of ten, which is why the curve looks like a wall at 0.7 V.
Check B2. (a) A diode has Is = 10 nA at 25 °C. Find Is at 55 °C. (b) Why is the reverse current almost independent of the reverse voltage? (c) Which leaks more in reverse, Si or Ge, and why?
Unit 2 › The junction

B3 · Diode resistances, equivalent circuits, capacitances, switching

Practice · definitions from slides 84–100 A diode carries 2 mA at 0.7 V. Find its static (DC) resistance and its dynamic (AC) resistance at that point. Take η = 1.
Guess first: which of the two is larger?
Q-point: the DC operating point (VD, ID) where the diode sits with no signal. · Small signal: an AC wiggle small enough that the curve looks straight around the Q-point.

Static resistance is just the ratio at the point: RD = VD/ID. It is large in reverse and at the knee, small higher up.

Dynamic resistance is the slope seen by a small AC signal riding on the DC point. Differentiating the Shockley equation:

rd = dVD/dID = ηVT/ID ≈ 26 mV / ID

Average AC resistance rav = ΔVD/ΔID between two points is used for large swings.

Equivalent circuits. Replace the curve with straight lines. The simplified model (a closed switch in series with 0.7 V when on, an open switch when off) is the one used in every circuit question unless the question says "ideal".

CapacitanceWhenFormulaCause
Transition (depletion) CTreverse biasCT = εA/WThe depletion region is an insulator between two conducting plates. More reverse voltage → wider W → smaller CT. A varactor uses this.
Diffusion (storage) CDforward biasCD = τID/ηVTInjected minority carriers are stored near the junction; the stored charge grows with current. Much larger than CT.

Switching. A conducting diode cannot turn off at once. When the voltage reverses, the stored minority carriers keep a large reverse current flowing for the storage time ts, then it decays over the transition time tt. Their sum is the reverse recovery time trr = ts + tt, from nanoseconds to a few microseconds. It limits the highest usable frequency.

Answer. RD = 0.7 V / 2 mA = 350 Ω. rd = 26 mV / 2 mA = 13 Ω. The curve is steep at that point, so a small change in voltage gives a large change in current.
Check B3. (a) Find rd at ID = 0.5 mA and at 5 mA. (b) Which capacitance matters in reverse bias, and how does it change as the reverse voltage grows? (c) What physically causes the reverse recovery time?
Unit 2 › Diode circuits

B4 · Load line and DC diode circuits

Professor's deck L08 · slide 4 · Example For the given diode configuration and diode characteristics, determine: VDQ, IDQ and VR. (E = 10 V, R = 0.5 kΩ, silicon diode.)
Guess first: roughly how much of the 10 V lands on the resistor?

Load line. The diode and the resistor carry the same current, and KVL gives E = VD + IDR. Rearranged, ID = (E − VD)/R is a straight line on the diode's own axes. Find its two ends: VD = 0 gives ID = E/R; ID = 0 gives VD = E. The circuit must sit on the line and on the diode curve at once, so the answer is where they cross: the Q-point.

Answer. Ends: E/R = 10/0.5 k = 20 mA and E = 10 V. The crossing reads VDQ ≈ 0.78 V, IDQ ≈ 18.5 mA. VR = IDQR = 18.5 mA × 0.5 kΩ = 9.25 V (check: E − VDQ = 9.22 V, the same within reading error).
Slip in the slide. Slide 5 writes VR = (18.5 mA)(1 K) = 18.5 V. R is 0.5 kΩ, and 18.5 V cannot come out of a 10 V source. Use 9.25 V.

Without the graph: the three-step method. Used for every other circuit on these slides.

  1. Decide the state. Mentally remove the diode. If the voltage that appears across the gap would push current in the direction of the arrow and is more than 0.7 V (Si), the diode is ON. Otherwise it is OFF.
  2. Substitute. ON → a 0.7 V drop (0.3 V for Ge, 0 for ideal). OFF → an open circuit, I = 0.
  3. Solve with KVL and Ohm's law.

Worked (deck L08, slide 14): determine I, V1, V2 and Vo. The sources total 15 V around the loop and push current along the arrow, so the diode is ON. I = (10 + 5 − 0.7)/(4.7 k + 2.2 k) = 2.07 mA. V1 = IR1 = 9.74 V. V2 = IR2 = 4.56 V. Vo = V2 + E2 = 4.56 − 5 = −0.44 V.

Rules for combinations. Diodes in series: the drops add (Si + red LED = 0.7 + 1.8 V). A reversed diode anywhere in a series path opens the path. Diodes in parallel: the voltage across the pair is one drop, 0.7 V, and identical diodes share the current equally.

Check B4. All from deck L08. (a) Slide 9: E = 8 V, a Si diode and R = 2.2 kΩ in series. Find VD, VR, ID. Then reverse the diode and repeat. (b) Slide 12: +12 V feeds a Si diode, then a red LED (1.8 V), then 680 Ω to ground. Vo is across the resistor. Find Vo and ID. (c) Slide 15: 10 V feeds 0.33 kΩ, then two Si diodes in parallel to ground. Find Vo (across the diodes), I1 (through the resistor) and the current in each diode. (d) Slide 18: a 20 V source feeds Si diode D1 in series; then R1 = 3.3 kΩ sits in parallel with Si diode D2; then R2 = 5.6 kΩ returns to the source. Find I1 (in R1), I2 (in R2) and ID2.
Unit 2 › Diode circuits

B5 · Rectifiers

Professor's deck L09 · slide 9 · Example Sketch dc output vo and determine the dc level of the output. Repeat if the ideal diode is replaced by silicon diode. (Input: sine wave of 20 V peak. The diode points toward the source, with R = 2 kΩ across the output.)
Guess first: which half-cycle reaches the output, and with what sign?
Rectifier: a circuit that turns AC into one-direction (pulsating DC) voltage. · Vm: the peak of the input sine. Vrms = Vm/√2. · Vdc: the average of the output over one period, which is what a DC voltmeter reads.

Half-wave. One diode. It conducts on one half-cycle and blocks the other. Averaging one half-sine over a full period: Vdc = Vm/π = 0.318 Vm. With a real Si diode the peak is lower: Vdc ≈ 0.318(Vm − 0.7).

PIV (peak inverse voltage) is the largest reverse voltage the diode must survive while blocking. Its rating must exceed this. Half-wave: PIV = Vm.

Full-wave bridge (left). Four diodes. On the positive half D1 and D3 conduct; on the negative half D2 and D4. Either way, current goes through R in the same direction, so both halves are used: Vdc = 2Vm/π = 0.636 Vm. Two diodes are in the path, so with Si diodes Vdc ≈ 0.636(Vm − 1.4).

Centre-tapped full-wave (right). Two diodes and a transformer whose secondary has a middle tap. Each half of the secondary feeds R through its own diode on alternate half-cycles. Vm here is the peak from the tap to one end. The off diode sees both halves, so PIV = 2Vm.

Half-waveCentre-tappedBridge
Diodes124
Vdc (ideal)0.318 Vm0.636 Vm0.636 Vm
Vdc (Si diodes)0.318(Vm − 0.7)0.636(Vm − 0.7)0.636(Vm − 1.4)
Vrms of outputVm/2Vm/√2Vm/√2
PIV per diodeVm2VmVm
Ripple factor r1.210.4820.482
Max efficiency η40.6%81.2%81.2%
Ripple frequencyf2f2f

Ripple factor measures how much AC is left in the output: r = (rms of the AC part)/Vdc = √[(Vrms/Vdc)² − 1]. Smaller is better. Efficiency is DC power delivered over AC power drawn: η = (Vdc/Vrms)² for ideal diodes. A capacitor across R (a filter) holds the voltage up between peaks and cuts the ripple.

Answer. The diode points toward the source, so it conducts only when vi is negative: the output is the negative half-cycles. Ideal: Vdc = −0.318 × 20 = −6.36 V. Silicon: Vdc = −0.318 × (20 − 0.7) = −6.14 V. PIV = 20 V.
Check B5. (a) Derive the ripple factor 1.21 of a half-wave rectifier from Vrms = Vm/2 and Vdc = Vm/π. (b) A bridge rectifier with Si diodes is fed 12 V rms. Find Vm, Vdc and the PIV. (c) Why is a bridge usually preferred over the centre-tapped circuit? Give two reasons.
Unit 2 › Diode circuits

B6 · Clippers

Professor's deck L10 · slide 3 · Example Determine the output waveform for the network. (Series clipper: a 5 V battery, then an ideal diode, then R. Input: sine wave of 20 V peak.)
Guess first: sketch vo for one cycle.
Clipper (limiter): a circuit that removes part of a waveform and passes the rest unchanged. · Transition voltage: the input value at which the diode changes state.

Series clipper: the diode is in series with the output, so the output exists only while the diode conducts. A battery in series shifts the level at which it starts.

  1. Find the transition voltage. Set the ideal diode at the edge of conduction (id = 0, vd = 0) and write KVL. Here vi + 5 = 0, so the diode switches at vi = −5 V.
  2. Diode ON (vi > −5 V): KVL gives vo = vi + 5.
  3. Diode OFF (vi < −5 V): no current, so vo = 0.
Answer. The output is the input lifted by 5 V while vi > −5 V, and zero otherwise. Its peak is 20 + 5 = 25 V.

Parallel clipper: the diode is across the output. While it is OFF the output simply follows the input. While it is ON it pins the output to the battery level. Worked (deck L10, slide 6): triangular input of 16 V peak, ideal diode with its anode on a 4 V battery. The diode conducts whenever vi < 4 V and holds vo = 4 V. Above 4 V it is off and vo = vi. With a silicon diode (slide 7) the pinned level becomes 4 − 0.7 = 3.3 V.

Two such branches facing opposite ways clip both peaks, which squares up a sine wave.

Check B6. (a) In the series clipper above, reverse the battery. Find the new transition voltage and the peak of vo. (b) In the parallel clipper, turn the diode around (cathode on the battery). Describe vo. (c) In which clipper type does the output follow the input while the diode is off?
Unit 2 › Diode circuits

B7 · Clampers and voltage multipliers

Professor's deck L10 · slide 13 · Example Determine vo for the network. (Square wave input, +10 V and −20 V, f = 1000 Hz. C = 0.1 μF, R = 100 kΩ, ideal diode in series with a 5 V battery.)
Guess first: the input swings 30 V in total. What total swing will the output have?
Clamper: a capacitor, a diode and a resistor that shift a whole waveform up or down without changing its shape. · Time constant τ = RC: a capacitor needs about 5τ to charge or discharge fully.

How it works. On one half-cycle the diode conducts and charges C quickly to a fixed voltage. On the other half-cycle the diode is off, and C can only discharge through the large R. If 5τ is much longer than the half-period, C holds its voltage and acts like a battery in series with the input. That battery is the shift.

  1. Start with the half-cycle that turns the diode ON. Here that is vi = −20 V. With the diode a short, the output is pinned to the battery: vo = 5 V.
  2. Find VC from KVL in that state: −20 + VC − 5 = 0, so VC = 25 V.
  3. Other half-cycle, diode OFF, C keeps 25 V: vo = vi + VC = 10 + 25 = 35 V.
  4. Check the swing. Output swing = input swing: 35 − 5 = 30 V. ✓
Answer. vo is a square wave between 5 V and 35 V. The hold condition is met: τ = RC = 100 kΩ × 0.1 μF = 10 ms, so 5τ = 50 ms, which is 100 times the half-period T/2 = 0.5 ms.

Voltage multipliers chain clampers and peak detectors to give a DC output of several times the input peak.

Half-wave doubler. Positive half: D1 conducts and charges C1 to Vm. Negative half: the source and C1 add in series, D2 conducts, and C2 charges to 2Vm (top plate negative). Each diode must stand PIV = 2Vm.

Adding more diode–capacitor sections gives a tripler (3Vm) and a quadrupler (4Vm). They suit high-voltage, low-current loads.

Check B7. (a) In the example, remove the 5 V battery (diode straight to ground). Find the two output levels. (b) What goes wrong if R is made 100 Ω? (c) What DC voltage does a quadrupler give from a 10 V peak input, ideally?
Unit 2 › Breakdown

B8 · Breakdown, the Zener regulator, the Schottky diode

Practice · Zener regulator, fixed Vi and R In the regulator shown, Vi = 16 V, R = 1 kΩ, VZ = 10 V. Find VL, IL, IZ and PZ for (a) RL = 1.2 kΩ and (b) RL = 3 kΩ.
Guess first: in which case is the Zener actually regulating?

Breakdown is the sharp rise of reverse current at a certain reverse voltage. It does not destroy the diode if the current is limited. Two mechanisms:

Zener breakdownAvalanche breakdown
Dopingheavy on both sideslight
Depletion regionvery thin, so the field is enormouswide
Mechanismthe field pulls electrons straight out of their bonds (tunnelling)carriers gain enough speed to knock other electrons out of bonds; each new carrier does the same (multiplication)
Breakdown voltagebelow about 5 Vabove about 6 V
As temperature risesbreakdown voltage falls (negative coefficient)breakdown voltage rises (positive coefficient)

Zener diode. A diode built to work in breakdown. There its voltage stays almost fixed at VZ over a wide range of current, so it is used as a voltage reference.

  1. Test the state. Remove the Zener and find the voltage across RL: V = ViRL/(R + RL). If V ≥ VZ the Zener is ON. If not, it is OFF and acts as an open circuit.
  2. If ON: VL = VZ. IR = (Vi − VZ)/R. IL = VZ/RL. IZ = IR − IL. PZ = VZIZ, which must stay below the rating PZM.
Answer. (a) V = 16 × 1.2/2.2 = 8.73 V < 10 V, so the Zener is OFF: VL = 8.73 V, IZ = 0, PZ = 0. No regulation. (b) V = 16 × 3/4 = 12 V ≥ 10 V, so it is ON: VL = 10 V, IR = 6/1 k = 6 mA, IL = 10/3 k = 3.33 mA, IZ = 6 − 3.33 = 2.67 mA, PZ = 26.7 mW. The smallest load that keeps it on is RL,min = RVZ/(Vi − VZ) = 1.67 kΩ.

Schottky diode. A junction between a metal and n-type silicon instead of p and n. Only majority carriers (electrons) take part, so there is no stored minority charge and almost no reverse recovery time: it switches very fast. Its forward drop is low, about 0.2–0.4 V. The price is a larger reverse leakage and a lower breakdown voltage. Used in high-frequency rectifiers and fast logic.

Check B8. (a) A 4.7 V Zener and a 12 V Zener heat up. Which one's voltage falls, and why? (b) In the example, Vi rises to 20 V with RL = 3 kΩ. Find IZ. (c) Why can a Schottky diode switch faster than a pn diode?
Unit 2 › Special diodes (taught on the slides)

B9 · LED, photodiode, tunnel diode

Practice · from the deck "LED, Tunnel, Photo" Draw the V–I characteristic of a tunnel diode and explain the negative-resistance region.
Guess first: what would "negative resistance" have to mean on an I–V graph?
DeviceBiasWhat happensKey facts
LEDforwardElectrons and holes recombine at the junction and each recombination releases a photon. Needs a direct-gap material (GaAs, GaAsP, GaN), not Si. The colour is set by the gap: λ(μm) = 1.24/Eg(eV). Forward drop 1.8–3.3 V. Always used with a series resistor.
PhotodiodereverseLight falling on the depletion region generates electron–hole pairs, which the field sweeps out as extra reverse current. Current is proportional to light intensity. The small current with no light is the dark current. A PIN photodiode has an undoped (intrinsic) layer between p and n that widens the depletion region: more light absorbed, less capacitance, faster.
Tunnel (Esaki) diodesmall forwardDoping is about 1000 times heavier than normal, so the depletion region is only about 10 nm thick. Electrons pass straight through the barrier (tunnelling). Shows negative resistance. Very fast. Used in microwave oscillators and fast switches.
Answer. As the forward voltage rises from zero, filled states on the n side line up with empty states on the p side and tunnel current rises to the peak Ip at Vp. Raising the voltage further pulls those states out of line, so fewer electrons can tunnel and the current falls to the valley Iv at Vv. Between peak and valley the current falls while the voltage rises, so dI/dV is negative: negative resistance. Beyond the valley, ordinary diode current takes over and rises again.
Check B9. (a) Why can't silicon make a useful LED? (b) A red LED material has Eg = 1.9 eV. Find the wavelength. (c) Which of the three devices works in reverse bias, and what carries its current?

Answers: Part B Checks

  1. B1. (a) Vbi = 0.0259 × ln(10³³/10²⁰) = 0.0259 × 29.9 = 0.774 V. (b) The n side: it is more lightly doped, so it needs more width to hold the same charge. (c) Diffusion of majority carriers across the junction and drift of minority carriers back, driven by the built-in field.
  2. B2. (a) 30 °C is three doublings: 10 × 2³ = 80 nA. (b) It is made of minority carriers generated by heat; their supply depends on temperature, not on the voltage. (c) Ge. Its smaller gap gives a far larger ni, and Is ∝ ni².
  3. B3. (a) 26 mV/0.5 mA = 52 Ω; 26 mV/5 mA = 5.2 Ω. (b) Transition capacitance CT = εA/W; it falls, because W widens. (c) Minority carriers stored near the junction during conduction must be removed before the diode can block.
  4. B4. (a) Forward: VD = 0.7 V, VR = 7.3 V, ID = 7.3/2.2 k = 3.32 mA. Reversed: ID = 0, VR = 0, VD = 8 V (all the source voltage sits across the open diode). (b) Vo = 12 − 0.7 − 1.8 = 9.5 V; ID = 9.5/680 = 13.97 mA. (c) Vo = 0.7 V; I1 = (10 − 0.7)/0.33 k = 28.18 mA; each diode carries 14.09 mA. (d) R1 has D2's 0.7 V across it: I1 = 0.7/3.3 k = 0.212 mA. KVL round the loop: I2 = (20 − 0.7 − 0.7)/5.6 k = 3.32 mA. ID2 = I2 − I1 = 3.11 mA.
  5. B5. (a) Vrms/Vdc = (Vm/2)/(Vm/π) = π/2 = 1.571; r = √(1.571² − 1) = 1.21. (b) Vm = 12√2 = 17.0 V; Vdc = 0.636 × (17.0 − 1.4) = 9.92 V; PIV ≈ 17 V. (c) No centre-tapped transformer is needed, and each diode needs only half the PIV rating (Vm instead of 2Vm).
  6. B6. (a) KVL at the edge: vi − 5 = 0, so the diode switches at +5 V. ON for vi > 5 V with vo = vi − 5; peak 15 V. (b) The diode now conducts when vi > 4 V and pins vo = 4 V; below 4 V, vo = vi. The top is clipped at 4 V. (c) The parallel clipper.
  7. B7. (a) Diode ON at −20 V pins vo = 0 and VC = 20 V; other half vo = 10 + 20 = 30 V. Levels 0 V and 30 V. (b) τ = 100 Ω × 0.1 μF = 10 μs, far shorter than 0.5 ms. C discharges within each half-cycle, so the level droops and the wave shape is distorted. (c) 40 V.
  8. B8. (a) The 4.7 V one. Below about 5 V the mechanism is Zener breakdown, which has a negative temperature coefficient. The 12 V diode is avalanche and its voltage rises. (b) IR = (20 − 10)/1 k = 10 mA; IL = 3.33 mA; IZ = 6.67 mA. (c) Its current is carried by majority carriers only, so no minority charge is stored and nothing has to be cleared at turn-off.
  9. B9. (a) Si has an indirect gap: recombination goes through traps and gives heat, not light. (b) λ = 1.24/1.9 = 0.653 μm = 653 nm (red). (c) The photodiode. Electron–hole pairs generated by light in the depletion region.
Part C · Unit 3

The JFET

A diode has two terminals and no control. A transistor adds a third terminal that controls the current between the other two. The JFET is the simplest one to understand: a reverse-biased pn junction (Part B) squeezes a channel of doped silicon (Part A).

Unit 3 › Device

C1 · Construction and operation

Practice · JFET deck slides 5–16 Why is a JFET called a voltage-controlled device, and why is its input resistance so high?
Guess first: the gate junction is reverse biased. How much gate current flows?
Channel: the strip of n-type silicon that current flows through. · Source, Drain: the two ends of the channel; carriers enter at the source and leave at the drain. · Gate: the p regions on both sides of the channel, joined together.

Construction (n-channel). A bar of n-type silicon with a contact at each end (source and drain). Two heavily doped p regions are diffused into its sides and wired together as the gate. Each p region forms a pn junction with the channel, and every junction has a depletion region (B1).

Operation. The gate is always reverse biased (VGS ≤ 0 for n-channel). Making VGS more negative widens the depletion regions (B1), which narrows the channel and raises its resistance, so the drain current ID falls. At VGS = VGS(off) the depletion regions meet, the channel is closed and ID = 0.

Pinch-off. With VGS = 0, raise VDS. The drain end of the channel is more positive than the source end, so the reverse bias, and the depletion region, is widest near the drain. At VDS = VP, the pinch-off voltage, the regions almost touch at the drain end. Beyond this the current stops rising and stays at IDSS: the drain-to-source saturation current, which is the largest current the JFET can carry. Numerically VP = |VGS(off)|.

p-channel: swap n and p, reverse every voltage and current direction; holes carry the current.

Answer. The drain current is set by the gate voltage VGS through the width of the depletion regions; no gate current is needed. The gate junction is reverse biased, so only a leakage current of nanoamps flows (IG ≈ 0). Input resistance = VGS/IG is therefore very high, 10⁸–10¹² Ω. Also, only one type of carrier takes part (electrons in an n-channel device), so the JFET is a unipolar device.
Check C1. (a) What two things does making VGS more negative do inside the device? (b) Define IDSS and VGS(off). (c) Why is the depletion region wider at the drain end than at the source end?
Unit 3 › Device

C2 · Characteristics and Shockley's equation

Professor's JFET numericals sheet · Q2 A JFET has the following parameters: IDSS = 32 mA; VGS(off) = −8 V; VGS = −4.5 V. Find the value of drain current.
Guess first: VGS is a little over halfway to cutoff. Is ID more or less than half of IDSS?

Drain curves (right): ID against VDS, one curve per VGS. Four regions:

RegionCondition (n-channel)Behaviour
OhmicVDS < VGS − VGS(off)ID rises with VDS. The channel is a resistor whose value is set by VGS (a voltage-variable resistor).
Saturation (pinch-off, active)VDS ≥ VGS − VGS(off)ID is constant, set only by VGS. Amplifiers work here.
CutoffVGS ≤ VGS(off)ID = 0.
BreakdownVDS too largeThe gate junction avalanches; ID shoots up.

Transfer curve (left): ID against VGS in saturation. It is a parabola, given by Shockley's equation:

ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VGS(off))²

Quick points for sketching it: VGS = 0 → IDSS. VGS = VGS(off)/2 → IDSS/4. VGS = VGS(off) → 0. Keep the signs: for an n-channel JFET both VGS and VGS(off) are negative, so the ratio is positive.

Answer. ID = 32 × (1 − (−4.5)/(−8))² = 32 × (0.4375)² = 6.12 mA. That is under a fifth of IDSS: the square makes the current fall quickly.
Check C2. From the same sheet. (a) Q3: A JFET has a drain current of 5 mA. If IDSS = 10 mA and VGS(off) = −6 V, find the value of (i) VGS and (ii) VP. (b) Q5: VGS = −2 V, VGS(off) = −6 V, IDSS = 3 mA. Determine the drain current. (c) Q4: VGS(off) = −4 V, IDSS = 12 mA, RD = 560 Ω, gate tied to source (VGS = 0). Determine the minimum VDD that puts the device in the constant-current region.
Unit 3 › Device · flagged "8 marks"

C3 · The characteristic parameters: gm, rd, gd, μ

Professor's JFET deck · slides 30–31 "Characteristics parameters of JFET" · a classmate's relay says 8 marks Define the characteristic parameters of a JFET and derive the relation among them.
Guess first: ID depends on two voltages. How many independent slopes can you define?
ParameterDefinitionHeld constantMeaning · unit
Transconductance (mutual conductance) gmgm = ΔID/ΔVGSVDSHow strongly the gate voltage controls the drain current. Slope of the transfer curve. Siemens (mS, μS; also written mho).
Drain resistance rdrd = ΔVDS/ΔIDVGSAC resistance of the channel in saturation. Inverse slope of a drain curve. Tens of kΩ to MΩ.
Drain conductance gdgd = ΔID/ΔVDS = 1/rdVGSSlope of a drain curve. Siemens.
Amplification factor μμ = −ΔVDS/ΔVGSIDHow many volts of VDS are needed to undo 1 V of VGS. No unit.
Derivation of μ = gm rd. ID is a function of VGS and VDS. For small changes (Taylor's theorem, first-order terms):

ΔID = (∂ID/∂VGS)ΔVGS + (∂ID/∂VDS)ΔVDS = gmΔVGS + ΔVDS/rd

Hold ID constant, so ΔID = 0: gmΔVGS = −ΔVDS/rd. Therefore −ΔVDS/ΔVGS = gmrd, and by definition the left side is μ:

μ = gm × rd

gm from Shockley's equation. Differentiate ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VGS(off))² with respect to VGS:

gm = gm0(1 − VGS/VGS(off))     gm0 = 2IDSS/|VGS(off)|     gm = gm0√(ID/IDSS)

gm0 is the value at VGS = 0, the largest gm the device has. gm falls in a straight line to zero at cutoff. Example: IDSS = 8 mA, VGS(off) = −4 V gives gm0 = 4 mS; at VGS = −2 V, gm = 2 mS. With rd = 50 kΩ, μ = 2 mS × 50 kΩ = 100.

Check C3. From the sheet. (a) Q7: When VGS of a JFET changes from −3.1 V to −3 V, the drain current changes from 1 mA to 1.3 mA. What is the value of transconductance? (b) Q8: A JFET has a value of gm0 = 4000 μS. Determine the value of gm at VGS = −3 V. Given that VGS(off) = −8 V. (c) Write μ = gmrd starting from ΔID = 0, from memory.
Unit 3 › Circuits

C4 · Biasing the JFET

Professor's JFET numericals sheet · Q17 Determine ID and VGS for the JFET with voltage-divider bias in Fig. 9, given that VD = 7 V.
Guess first: which single resistor lets you find ID straight away?
Biasing: choosing the DC voltages and resistors so the transistor sits at a wanted Q-point (ID, VDS) in saturation. · VG, VS, VD: voltages from each terminal to ground. VGS = VG − VS.

Two facts make every JFET bias problem short: IG = 0, so no current and no voltage drop in the gate resistor, and IS = ID.

CircuitGate-source loopNotes
Fixed biasVGS = −VGGA separate negative supply sets VGS directly. Then Shockley gives ID. Needs two supplies.
Self-bias (right)VG = 0, VS = IDRS, so VGS = −IDRSThe drop across RS makes the source positive, which is the same as making the gate negative. One supply. If ID rises, VGS gets more negative and pulls it back: self-correcting.
Voltage divider (left)VG = VDDR2/(R1 + R2), VGS = VG − IDRSMost stable Q-point. VGS must still come out negative.

In every case the drain loop gives VDS = VDD − ID(RD + RS).

Worked self-bias (right-hand circuit, IDSS = 8 mA, VGS(off) = −4 V). Put VGS = −IDRS = −ID (mA, kΩ) into Shockley: ID = 8(1 − ID/4)², which rearranges to ID² − 10ID + 16 = 0, so ID = 2 mA or 8 mA. Reject 8 mA: it would need VGS = −8 V, beyond cutoff. So ID = 2 mA, VGS = −2 V, VDS = 20 − 2(3.3 + 1) = 11.4 V. Saturation check: 11.4 ≥ VGS − VGS(off) = 2 V ✓.

Answer (Q17). VD is given, so use RD: ID = (VDD − VD)/RD = (12 − 7)/3.3 k = 1.52 mA. VS = IDRS = 1.52 mA × 1.8 kΩ = 2.73 V. VG = 12 × 1/(6.8 + 1) = 1.54 V. VGS = 1.54 − 2.73 = −1.19 V (the sheet rounds to −1.2 V).
Check C4. From the sheet. (a) Q18: In an n-channel JFET biased by potential divider method, it is desired to set the operating point at ID = 2.5 mA and VDS = 8 V. If VDD = 30 V, R1 = 1 MΩ and R2 = 500 kΩ, find the value of RS. The parameters of JFET are IDSS = 10 mA and VGS(off) = −5 V. (b) Q19: a JFET amplifier has VDD = 20 V and RD = 500 Ω (no RS). Give the two end points of its d.c. load line.
Unit 3 › Circuits

C5 · Small-signal model and JFET amplifiers

Practice · JFET deck slides 35–44 A common-source JFET amplifier has gm = 2 mS, rd = 50 kΩ and RD = 2.2 kΩ, with the source resistor fully bypassed. Find the voltage gain.
Guess first: will the output be in phase with the input or inverted?
Coupling capacitor (C1, C2): passes the AC signal, blocks DC, so the bias is not disturbed. · Bypass capacitor (CS): shorts RS for AC so it does not reduce the gain. · AC equivalent circuit: capacitors and DC supplies replaced by short circuits.

Small-signal model (right). For small AC signals around the Q-point, the JFET is a voltage-controlled current source gmvgs in parallel with rd. The gate is an open circuit.

Common source (CS)Common drain (CD), source followerCommon gate (CG)
Input · outputgate · draingate · sourcesource · drain
Voltage gain Av−gm(rd ∥ RD)
unbypassed RS: −gmRD/(1 + gmRS)		gmRS/(1 + gmRS), just under 1+gm(rd ∥ RD) ≈ gmRD
Phaseinverted (180°)in phasein phase
Input impedance ZiRG (very high)RG (very high)RS ∥ 1/gm (low)
Output impedance Zord ∥ RD ≈ RDRS ∥ 1/gm (low)≈ RD
Used asvoltage amplifierbuffer between a high-resistance source and a low-resistance loadhigh-frequency amplifier; matches a low-impedance source

Why CS inverts: a rise in vgs raises id, which drops more voltage across RD, so the drain voltage falls.

Applications of the JFET: low-noise, high-input-impedance amplifier (first stage of instruments and receivers), buffer, voltage-variable resistor (ohmic region), analog switch and chopper, constant-current source (VGS = 0 gives IDSS).

Answer. rd ∥ RD = (50 × 2.2)/(52.2) = 2.107 kΩ. Av = −gm(rd ∥ RD) = −2 mS × 2.107 kΩ = −4.21. The minus sign means the output is inverted.
Check C5. (a) A source follower has gm = 2 mS and RS = 1 kΩ. Find Av and Zo. (b) What happens to the CS gain if the bypass capacitor CS is removed, and why? (c) Which configuration would you place between a 1 MΩ sensor and a 1 kΩ load?

Answers: Part C Checks

  1. C1. (a) Widens the gate depletion regions and so narrows the channel; channel resistance rises and ID falls. (b) IDSS: the drain current in saturation with VGS = 0, the maximum. VGS(off): the gate-source voltage at which ID becomes zero. (c) The channel voltage rises from source to drain, so the gate junction is more reverse biased near the drain.
  2. C2. (a) 5 = 10(1 + VGS/6)², so 1 + VGS/6 = √0.5 = 0.707 and VGS = −1.76 V. VP = |VGS(off)| = 6 V. (b) ID = 3(1 − 2/6)² = 3 × 0.444 = 1.33 mA. (c) Constant-current needs VDS ≥ VP = 4 V, with ID = IDSS = 12 mA. VDD = VDS + IDRD = 4 + 12 mA × 560 Ω = 10.72 V.
  3. C3. (a) gm = ΔID/ΔVGS = 0.3 mA/0.1 V = 3 mS = 3000 μS. (b) gm = 4000 × (1 − 3/8) = 2500 μS. (c) See the green box.
  4. C4. (a) Shockley: 2.5 = 10(1 + VGS/5)² gives 1 + VGS/5 = 0.5, VGS = −2.5 V. VG = 30 × 500/1500 = 10 V. VS = VG − VGS = 12.5 V. RS = 12.5 V/2.5 mA = 5 kΩ. (b) ID = 0: VDS = VDD = 20 V. VDS = 0: ID = VDD/RD = 40 mA.
  5. C5. (a) Av = 2/(1 + 2) = 0.667; Zo = 1 kΩ ∥ 500 Ω = 333 Ω. (b) It falls to −gmRD/(1 + gmRS): the signal current now flows through RS, and the voltage it develops there subtracts from vgs (negative feedback, Part F). (c) Common drain: very high Zi, low Zo.
Part D · Unit 4

The MOSFET

The JFET controls its channel with a reverse-biased junction. The MOSFET replaces that junction with a metal plate on a thin layer of glass. The idea is the same (a gate voltage sets the channel current), the equations are almost the same, and it is the transistor inside every digital chip.

Unit 4 › Device

D1 · Structure and types

Practice · MOSFET deck slides 4–18 With VGS = 0, an enhancement MOSFET carries no drain current but a depletion MOSFET does. Explain why.
Guess first: what would have to exist between source and drain for current to flow?
Oxide: a very thin insulating layer of SiO₂ under the gate. · Substrate (body): the p-type silicon the device is built in, normally tied to the source. · n⁺: heavily doped n-type.

Structure (n-channel enhancement, "nMOS"). Two n⁺ regions, source and drain, sit in a p-type substrate. Over the gap between them lies the oxide, and on top of it the gate electrode. Metal–Oxide–Semiconductor gives the name. The gate, oxide and substrate form a capacitor.

Operation. With VGS = 0 the path from drain to source is n–p–n: two diodes back to back, so no current. A positive gate voltage pushes holes away from the surface and attracts electrons. When VGS reaches the threshold voltage VT (also written VGS(th)), enough electrons gather under the oxide to form an n-type inversion layer: the channel. More gate voltage means more electrons and more current. The channel is enhanced by the gate, hence "enhancement type".

Enhancement MOSFET (E-MOSFET)Depletion MOSFET (D-MOSFET)
Channel at VGS = 0none; device is OFF ("normally off")built in during manufacture; device is ON ("normally on")
n-channel controlVGS > VT (positive) turns it onnegative VGS depletes the channel; positive VGS enhances it
Equation in saturationID = K(VGS − VT)²Shockley, as for a JFET: ID = IDSS(1 − VGS/VGS(off))², valid for positive VGS too
Symbolbroken channel linesolid channel line

p-channel (pMOS): n-type substrate, p⁺ source and drain, holes carry the current, and every voltage is reversed (VT is negative; it turns on when VGS < VT).

Compared with a JFET: the gate is insulated, so IG is practically zero and the input resistance is even higher (10¹⁰–10¹⁵ Ω). The thin oxide is easily destroyed by static charge, so MOSFETs need careful handling.

Answer. Current needs a continuous channel of one type between source and drain. An enhancement MOSFET has none at VGS = 0, only two back-to-back junctions, so it stays off until VGS exceeds VT and induces a channel. A depletion MOSFET is made with a channel already in place, so ID = IDSS flows at VGS = 0.
Check D1. (a) What does each letter of MOS stand for, and what does each layer do? (b) What is the inversion layer? (c) Why is the gate current of a MOSFET essentially zero?
Unit 4 › Device

D2 · Regions of operation and the current equations

Professor's numericals sheet · Q30 The data sheet for an E-MOSFET gives ID(on) = 500 mA at VGS = 10 V and VGS(th) = 1 V. Determine the drain current for VGS = 5 V.
Guess first: VGS is halved. Is the current halved?
RegionTest (n-channel)Drain currentActs as
CutoffVGS ≤ VTID = 0open switch
Triode (ohmic, linear)VGS > VT and VDS < VGS − VTID = K[2(VGS − VT)VDS − VDS²]resistor set by VGS; closed switch
Saturation (active)VGS > VT and VDS ≥ VGS − VTID = K(VGS − VT)²current source set by VGS; amplifier

The region test is the first step of every MOSFET problem. VGS − VT is called the overdrive voltage. In saturation the channel is pinched off at the drain end, exactly as in the JFET, so ID no longer depends on VDS.

The constant K (A/V²) is found from one data-sheet point: K = ID(on)/(VGS(on) − VT)². In terms of the device, K = ½μnCox(W/L): carrier mobility, oxide capacitance per unit area, and the width-to-length ratio of the channel. Sedra & Smith write kn = μnCox(W/L) = 2K, so their saturation equation reads ID = ½kn(VGS − VT)². Same physics, different letter.

Channel-length modulation. The real curves tilt up slightly in saturation: ID = K(VGS − VT)²(1 + λVDS). This gives the output resistance ro = 1/(λID).

Answer. K = 500 mA/(10 − 1)² = 500/81 = 6.17 mA/V². At VGS = 5 V: ID = 6.17 × (5 − 1)² = 98.8 mA (the sheet prints 98.7). Halving VGS cut the current by five, because the law is a square of (VGS − VT).
Check D2. (a) Sheet Q26: For a certain D-MOSFET, IDSS = 10 mA and VGS(off) = −8 V. (i) Is this an n-channel or a p-channel? (ii) Calculate ID at VGS = −3 V. (iii) Calculate ID at VGS = +3 V. (b) An nMOS has K = 1 mA/V² and VT = 1 V, with VGS = 3 V. Name the region and find ID for VDS = 1 V and for VDS = 4 V.
Unit 4 › Circuits

D3 · Biasing the MOSFET

Practice · circuits from the "MOSFET biasing" deck, slides 10–16 For circuit (a), the E-MOSFET has K = 0.5 mA/V² and VT = 2 V. Find ID, VGS and VDS, and confirm the region.
Guess first: what is the gate voltage?

As with the JFET, IG = 0 and IS = ID. An n-channel E-MOSFET needs a positive VGS above VT.

CircuitGate-source loopNotes
Gate (fixed) biasVGS = VGGAn external source fixes VGS. Simple but the Q-point moves if K or VT change.
Voltage divider (a)VG = VDDR2/(R1 + R2); VGS = VG − IDRSGood stability; the usual choice.
Drain-to-gate feedback (b)no drop in RG, so VGS = VDS = VDD − IDRDSelf-stabilising, and always in saturation because VDS = VGS > VGS − VT.
Self-biasVGS = −IDRS (negative)Works only for a depletion MOSFET. A negative VGS can never turn on an n-channel enhancement device.
  1. Write VGS from the gate-source loop, in terms of ID.
  2. Substitute into ID = K(VGS − VT)² and solve the quadratic. Keep the root that gives VGS > VT.
  3. VDS = VDD − ID(RD + RS). Check VDS ≥ VGS − VT.

DC load line (slide 16): VDS = VDD − IDRD. Ends at (0, VDD/RD) and (VDD, 0). The Q-point is where it crosses the drain curve for the biased VGS.

Answer. VG = 20 × 3/(7 + 3) = 6 V. VGS = 6 − ID (mA, kΩ). ID = 0.5(6 − ID − 2)² = 0.5(4 − ID)², which gives ID² − 10ID + 16 = 0, so ID = 2 or 8 mA. 8 mA would make VGS = −2 V, below VT: reject. ID = 2 mA, VGS = 4 V, VDS = 20 − 2(3 + 1) = 12 V. Region: 12 ≥ 4 − 2 = 2 V, saturation ✓.
Check D3. (a) Solve circuit (b) with the same MOSFET (K = 0.5 mA/V², VT = 2 V). (b) Sheet Q28: a D-MOSFET with VGS(off) = −8 V and IDSS = 12 mA has its gate at 0 V, VDD = +18 V and RD = 620 Ω. Determine VDS. (c) Why does self-bias fail for an enhancement MOSFET?

Unit 4 › Applications

D5 · The MOSFET as a switch and CMOS logic gates

Professor's deck "MOSFET biasing and digital circuit" · slide 9 · "Complex Logic Gates in CMOS: Example" Implement f = (a·(b + c))′ as a single CMOS gate. How many transistors does it need?
Guess first: sketch the nMOS part, the network that must connect the output to ground when a·(b + c) = 1.
Logic 1 / 0: VDD / 0 V. · Pull-up network: transistors between VDD and the output. · Pull-down network: transistors between the output and ground.

Switch. Drive the gate fully on or fully off and the MOSFET is a switch: cutoff = open; triode with a large VGS = closed, with a small on-resistance rDS(on) ≈ 1/[2K(VGS − VT)]. It needs no gate current to stay on, which is why it suits digital circuits.

nMOS and pMOS are complementary switches. An nMOS closes when its gate is 1; a pMOS closes when its gate is 0. An nMOS passes a strong 0 but a weak 1 (the output stops at VDD − VT); a pMOS passes a strong 1 but a weak 0. So CMOS uses pMOS to pull up to VDD and nMOS to pull down to ground.

CMOS inverter. One pMOS on top, one nMOS below, gates joined. Input 0: pMOS on, nMOS off, output = VDD. Input 1: nMOS on, pMOS off, output = 0. In either steady state one transistor is off, so no current flows from VDD to ground: static power is nearly zero. Power is used only while switching. The output swings the full 0 to VDD.

Rules for any CMOS gate. The pull-down network of nMOS implements the function before the final inversion: transistors in series = AND, in parallel = OR. The pull-up network of pMOS is its dual: every series becomes parallel and every parallel becomes series. Each input drives one nMOS and one pMOS, so a gate with n inputs uses 2n transistors. A CMOS gate always inverts: NAND and NOR are natural, AND needs a NAND followed by an inverter.

Answer. Pull-down (nMOS): a in series with (b parallel c). Pull-up (pMOS), the dual: a in parallel with (b in series with c). Three inputs, so 6 transistors: 3 nMOS + 3 pMOS (right-hand circuit above). For every one of the 8 input combinations exactly one network conducts.
Check D5. (a) In a 2-input CMOS NOR, which transistors are in series and which in parallel? (b) Why does a CMOS inverter draw almost no current when its input is steady? (c) An nMOS with VT = 1 V and its gate at VDD = 5 V passes a logic 1. What voltage comes out? (d) Find rDS(on) for K = 0.5 mA/V², VGS = 10 V, VT = 2 V.
Unit 4 › Beyond the planar MOSFET (taught on the slides)

D6 · FinFET

Practice · from the two FinFET decks What problems appear when a planar MOSFET is scaled down, and how does a FinFET overcome them?
Guess first: when the channel gets very short, what else besides the gate can influence it?

The problem: short-channel effects. As the channel length shrinks to tens of nanometres, the drain sits so close to the source that the drain's field reaches into the channel and the gate loses control. The results: the threshold voltage shifts (falls) with channel length and drain voltage; the subthreshold slope degrades, so the device no longer turns off sharply; the off-state leakage current IOFF rises. Standby power goes up and performance stops improving.

The fix: wrap the gate around the channel. In a FinFET (Fin Field-Effect Transistor) the channel is a thin vertical fin of silicon standing on the substrate, and the gate covers it on three sides. Current flows along the two side walls and the top of the fin. With the gate on three sides, it controls the whole thin body, so the drain cannot take over.

Planar MOSFETFinFET
Gateon one side of the channel (top)wraps three sides of a raised fin
Control of channelweakens at short lengthsstrong: short-channel effects suppressed
Leakage, standby powerhigh at small sizeslow
Speed, drive current per arealowerhigher; works at lower supply voltage
Channel dopingneededoptional, because the body is thin and fully controlled
Widthany valueset by fin height; made larger only by adding whole fins
Fabricationsimpler, cheapercomplex and costly; more parasitic capacitance; heat is harder to remove

Types: shorted-gate (SG), where the gates on both sides are joined and act as one, and independent-gate (IG), where the two side gates are driven separately so one can adjust the threshold. Fins must be spaced correctly: too close and neighbouring fins interfere, too far and area is wasted.

Answer. Scaling a planar MOSFET brings short-channel effects: threshold shift, a worse subthreshold slope and a higher off current, because the drain starts to control the channel. A FinFET raises the channel into a thin fin and wraps the gate around three sides. The gate regains control, so leakage falls, switching is faster and scaling can continue.
Check D6. (a) Name three short-channel effects. (b) On how many sides does the gate touch the channel in a planar MOSFET and in a FinFET? (c) Give two disadvantages of FinFETs.

Answers: Part D Checks

  1. D1. (a) Metal: the gate electrode. Oxide: the SiO₂ insulator. Semiconductor: the silicon in which the channel forms. (b) A thin layer of electrons at the surface of the p-type substrate, attracted by a positive gate; it is n-type, so it joins source to drain. (c) The oxide is an insulator, so only a capacitor-charging current can flow, none in steady state.
  2. D2. (a) (i) n-channel: VGS(off) is negative. (ii) ID = 10(1 − 3/8)² = 3.91 mA. (iii) ID = 10(1 + 3/8)² = 18.9 mA, larger than IDSS because positive VGS enhances the channel. (b) Overdrive = 2 V. VDS = 1 V < 2 V: triode, ID = 1 × [2(2)(1) − 1²] = 3 mA. VDS = 4 V ≥ 2 V: saturation, ID = 1 × 2² = 4 mA.
  3. D3. (a) VGS = VDS = 12 − 4ID. ID = 0.5(10 − 4ID)² gives 8ID² − 41ID + 50 = 0, so ID = 2 mA or 3.125 mA. The second gives VGS = −0.5 V: reject. ID = 2 mA, VGS = VDS = 4 V. (b) VGS = 0, so ID = IDSS = 12 mA. VDS = 18 − 12 mA × 0.62 kΩ = 10.56 V (the sheet prints 10.6 V). (c) Self-bias makes VGS = −IDRS, which is negative; an n-channel enhancement device needs VGS > VT > 0, so it never turns on.
  4. D4. (a) Rin = 1/gm = 500 Ω. (b) Av = 2/(1 + 2) = 0.667. (c) gm = 2√(K·ID) = 2√(0.5 × 8) = 4 mS: four times the current gives twice the gm.
  5. D5. (a) The two pMOS are in series (pull-up); the two nMOS are in parallel (pull-down). (b) One of its two transistors is always off, so there is no path from VDD to ground. (c) VDD − VT = 4 V, a weak 1. (d) rDS(on) = 1/[2 × 0.5 mA/V² × 8 V] = 125 Ω.
  6. D6. (a) Threshold-voltage shift, degraded subthreshold slope, increased off (leakage) current. (b) One; three. (c) Complex, costly fabrication; width only in whole-fin steps; higher parasitic capacitance; self-heating (any two).
Part E · Unit 5

The BJT and its amplifiers

The FETs of Parts C and D use one junction or an oxide to control a channel with a voltage. The bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is two pn junctions back to back, and a small current into the middle layer controls a large current through the device. The slides spend the most lectures on this unit: biasing, stability and h-parameters carry the numericals.

Unit 5 › Device

E1 · Construction and operation

Practice · decks L20–L21 Why is the base of a transistor made very thin and lightly doped, while the emitter is heavily doped?
Guess first: what should happen to electrons that the emitter sends into the base?
Emitter (E): the layer that supplies (emits) the carriers. · Base (B): the thin middle layer that controls them. · Collector (C): the layer that collects them.

Construction. Three layers, n–p–n or p–n–p, so two junctions: emitter–base (EB) and collector–base (CB). It looks like two diodes back to back, but the base is so thin that the two junctions interact. "Bipolar" because both electrons and holes take part.

Operation (npn, active region). The EB junction is forward biased, so the emitter injects electrons into the base. The base is thin and has few holes, so only about 1% of those electrons recombine there; that needs a small base current IB. The other 99% diffuse across the base and are swept into the collector by the field of the reverse-biased CB junction. That is IC.

IE = IC + IB

The base current sets how much charge the base can pass, so a small IB controls a large IC: the BJT is a current-controlled device. For pnp, swap n and p, reverse all voltages and currents; holes are the main carriers.

RegionEB junctionCB junctionBehaviour · use
ActiveforwardreverseIC = βIB, VBE ≈ 0.7 V (Si). Amplifier.
SaturationforwardforwardIC is limited by the external circuit, less than βIB. VCE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V. Closed switch.
CutoffreversereverseIC ≈ 0. Open switch.
Answer. The goal is for almost every carrier from the emitter to reach the collector. A thin, lightly doped base has few holes and gives the electrons little time to meet one, so very few recombine: IB is small and the current gain IC/IB is large. The emitter is heavily doped so that the forward EB current is almost entirely electrons injected into the base, not holes injected back into the emitter. The collector is the largest region because it dissipates the most heat.
Check E1. (a) State the bias of each junction in the active region. (b) IE = 5 mA and IB = 50 μA. Find IC. (c) Which regions are used when the transistor works as a switch?
Unit 5 › Device

E2 · The three connections and the gains α, β, γ

Practice · decks L22–L25 A transistor has β = 100 and ICBO = 20 nA. Find α and ICEO.
Guess first: is α slightly below 1 or slightly above?

A transistor has three terminals but an amplifier needs two input and two output wires, so one terminal is shared ("common") between input and output. That gives three connections.

Common base (CB)Common emitter (CE)Common collector (CC), emitter follower
Input · output terminalemitter · collectorbase · collectorbase · emitter
Current gainα = IC/IE, just under 1 (0.95–0.995)β = IC/IB, 50–400γ = IE/IB = 1 + β
Voltage gainhighhighjust under 1
Input resistancevery low (tens of Ω)medium (about 1 kΩ)very high
Output resistancevery highmedium to high (tens of kΩ)very low
Phase shift0°180°0°
Used forhigh-frequency stages; matching a low-resistance sourcegeneral amplification: the only one with both current and voltage gain, so the highest power gainbuffer; impedance matching

Relations. Substitute IE = IC + IB into the definitions:

β = α/(1 − α)     α = β/(1 + β)     γ = 1 + β = 1/(1 − α)

Leakage currents. The reverse-biased CB junction leaks a small current of minority carriers. ICBO (also ICO) is the collector-to-base current with the emitter open. In CE the transistor amplifies its own leakage: ICEO = (1 + β)ICBO is the collector current with the base open. Complete expressions:

IC = αIE + ICBO     IC = βIB + (1 + β)ICBO

Characteristics. Input curves (IB against VBE in CE, IE against VBE in CB) look like a forward diode. Output curves are IC against VCE (or VCB), one per input current, nearly flat in the active region (figure in E3).

Answer. α = β/(1 + β) = 100/101 = 0.990. ICEO = (1 + β)ICBO = 101 × 20 nA = 2.02 μA.
Check E2. (a) α = 0.98. Find β and γ. (b) Derive β = α/(1 − α). (c) Which connection would you use to drive an 8 Ω loudspeaker from a high-resistance stage, and why?
Unit 5 › Circuits

E3 · DC load line, Q-point and fixed bias

Professor's deck L26–27 · slide 15 · fixed-bias example (circuit (a) in E4: VCC = 12 V, RB = 240 kΩ, RC = 2.2 kΩ, β = 50) For the fixed-bias circuit, find IB, IC and VCE at the operating point, and the saturation current.
Guess first: which loop gives IB directly?
Operating (Q) point: the DC values (VCE, IC) with no signal applied. · DC analysis: every capacitor is an open circuit.

Fixed bias has one resistor RB from VCC to the base. Two loops:

  1. Base–emitter loop: VCC = IBRB + VBE, so IB = (VCC − 0.7)/RB.
  2. Active region: IC = βIB.
  3. Collector–emitter loop: VCE = VCC − ICRC.

Load line. Step 3 is a straight line on the output curves. Its ends: IC = 0 gives VCE = VCC (cutoff); VCE = 0 gives IC(sat) = VCC/RC (saturation). The Q-point is where the line crosses the curve for the actual IB. For the largest undistorted output swing, place Q near the middle of the line.

Moving the Q-point (slides 20–22): a larger IB slides Q up the line toward saturation. A larger RC lowers the top end, so the line gets flatter. A lower VCC shifts the whole line inward, parallel to itself.

Answer. IB = (12 − 0.7)/240 k = 47.08 μA. IC = 50 × 47.08 μA = 2.35 mA. VCE = 12 − 2.35 mA × 2.2 kΩ = 6.82 V. IC(sat) = 12/2.2 k = 5.45 mA. Q sits near the middle of the line: a good place for an amplifier.
Check E3. In the same circuit: (a) the transistor is replaced by one with β = 100. Find the new IC and VCE. What has happened? (b) Give the two end points of the load line if RC is changed to 4 kΩ.
Unit 5 › Circuits

E4 · Bias stabilisation, stability factor, the three bias circuits

Professor's deck L26–27 · slide 27 · emitter-bias example (circuit (b): VCC = 20 V, RB = 430 kΩ, RC = 2 kΩ, RE = 1 kΩ, β = 50) For the emitter-stabilised circuit, find IB, IC and VCE. Then find its stability factor S and compare with the fixed-bias circuit (a).
Guess first: Check E3 showed fixed bias is ruined by a change in β. What could RE do about it?

Why stabilise. Three things shift the Q-point as the transistor warms up or is replaced: ICO (= ICBO) doubles for every 10 °C rise; VBE falls about 2.5 mV per °C; β rises with temperature and varies widely between transistors of the same type. All three raise IC. More IC means more heat, which raises IC again: thermal runaway.

Stability factor. It measures how much IC changes when the leakage ICO changes, with β and VBE held constant. Smaller is better; the ideal is 1.

S = ∂IC/∂ICO     general result: S = (1 + β) / (1 − β·dIB/dIC)

The general result comes from differentiating IC = βIB + (1 + β)ICO with respect to IC. Two more factors are defined the same way: S′ = ∂IC/∂VBE and S″ = ∂IC/∂β.

CircuitBase currentdIB/dICStability factor S
(a) Fixed biasIB = (VCC − VBE)/RB01 + β (worst)
(b) Emitter biasIB = (VCC − VBE)/(RB + (β + 1)RE)−RE/(RB + RE)(1 + β)(1 + RB/RE) / (1 + β + RB/RE)
(c) Voltage dividerIB = (ETh − VBE)/(RTh + (β + 1)RE)−RE/(RTh + RE)same formula with RB → RTh (best: RTh is small)
Collector-to-base feedbackIB = (VCC − VBE)/(RB + (β + 1)RC)−RC/(RB + RC)(1 + β) / (1 + βRC/(RB + RC))

How RE stabilises. If IC rises, the drop across RE rises, which raises the emitter voltage and leaves less voltage to drive the base. IB falls and pulls IC back. This is negative feedback (Part F). In every circuit with RE: VCE = VCC − ICRC − IERE ≈ VCC − IC(RC + RE), and IC(sat) = VCC/(RC + RE).

Answer. IB = (20 − 0.7)/(430 k + 51 × 1 k) = 19.3/481 k = 40.1 μA. IC = 50 × 40.1 μA = 2.01 mA. IE = 51 × 40.1 μA = 2.05 mA. VCE = 20 − 2.01 × 2 − 2.05 × 1 = 13.94 V (13.97 V if IE ≈ IC is used). RB/RE = 430, so S = 51 × 431/(51 + 430) = 45.7. The fixed-bias circuit has S = 1 + β = 51. RE helps only a little here, because RB is so much larger than RE.

Voltage-divider bias, worked (circuit (c), β = 100). Exact: replace R1, R2 and VCC by their Thévenin equivalent as seen from the base: ETh = VCCR2/(R1 + R2) = 22 × 3.9/42.9 = 2.0 V, RTh = R1 ∥ R2 = 3.55 kΩ. IB = (2.0 − 0.7)/(3.55 k + 101 × 1.5 k) = 8.38 μA, IC = 0.84 mA, VCE = 22 − 0.838 × 10 − 0.846 × 1.5 = 12.35 V. S = 101 × (1 + 2.36)/(101 + 2.36) = 3.29. Approximate (valid when βRE ≥ 10R2; here 150 k ≥ 39 k ✓): ignore IB, so VB = ETh = 2.0 V, VE = VB − 0.7 = 1.3 V, IC ≈ IE = 1.3/1.5 k = 0.87 mA. β does not appear at all in the approximate answer: that is why this circuit is called β-independent.

Bias compensation uses a temperature-sensitive part to cancel the drift instead of feedback. Diode compensation: a forward-biased diode of the same material in the base circuit; its drop falls with temperature exactly as VBE does, so the two cancel. Thermistor (resistance falls as temperature rises) placed in the lower divider arm: as it heats, the base voltage drops and holds IC down. Sensistor (resistance rises with temperature) placed in the upper arm or in the emitter does the same.

Check E4. (a) Why is S = 1 + β for fixed bias? (b) In circuit (b), RB is replaced by a divider with RTh = 10 kΩ. Find the new S (β = 50, RE = 1 kΩ). (c) Name the three quantities whose drift moves the Q-point, and the direction each moves IC as temperature rises.
Unit 5 › Amplifier analysis

E5 · h-parameters and CE amplifier analysis

Professor's h-parameter numericals (book pp. 131–145) · Problem 9 A CE amplifier is driven by a voltage source of internal resistance Rs = 800 Ω. The load impedance is a resistance of 2 kΩ. The h-parameters are hie = 1.1 k, hfe = 50, hoe = 25 μmho, hre = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴. Compute the current gain Ai, input resistance Ri, voltage gain Av, output resistance Ro and output terminal resistance Rot. Also calculate power gain Ap. Using (a) exact analysis (b) approximate analysis. Compute % error in Ai.
Guess first: β is about 50. Will the current gain into a real load be exactly 50, more, or less?
Two-port network: a box with an input pair and an output pair of terminals. · Small-signal quantities (lower case: ib, vce): the AC parts only. · mho (℧) = siemens: unit of conductance, 1/Ω.

Definition. For small signals the transistor is treated as a two-port and described by two equations (CE shown):

vbe = hieib + hrevce      ic = hfeib + hoevce

ParameterNameMeasured withUnitTypical (CE)
hie = vbe/ibinput resistanceoutput shorted (vce = 0)Ω1.1 kΩ
hre = vbe/vcereverse voltage ratioinput open (ib = 0)none2.5 × 10⁻⁴
hfe = ic/ibforward current gain (≈ β)output shortednone50
hoe = ic/vceoutput admittanceinput opensiemens25 μS

They are called hybrid parameters because their units are mixed. The second subscript names the connection: e, b or c (hib, hfc, …). The same four formulas below work for all three connections with the matching set.

QuantityExact formulaApproximate (hoeRL < 0.1: drop hoe, hre)
Current gain Ai = iL/ib−hfe/(1 + hoeRL)−hfe
Input resistance Rihie + hreAiRLhie
Voltage gain Av = vo/viAiRL/Ri−hfeRL/hie

Gain from the source, Avs = vo/vsAvRi/(Ri + Rs)  ·  power gain Ap = AiAv  ·  Rot = Ro ∥ RL

Always in this order: Ai → Ri → Av → Yo, because each uses the one before. The minus signs are the CE phase reversal.

Answer. (a) Exact. Ai = −50/(1 + 25 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000) = −50/1.05 = −47.6. Ri = 1100 + (2.5 × 10⁻⁴)(−47.6)(2000) = 1100 − 23.8 = 1076.2 Ω. Av = (−47.6)(2000)/1076.2 = −88.5. Avs = −88.5 × 1076.2/(1076.2 + 800) = −50.75. Yo = 25 × 10⁻⁶ − (50)(2.5 × 10⁻⁴)/(1100 + 800) = 25 μS − 6.58 μS = 18.42 μS, so Ro = 54.28 kΩ. Rot = 54.28 k ∥ 2 k = 1.93 kΩ. Ap = AiAv = (−47.6)(−88.5) = 4214 (the book rounds earlier and prints 4210.6). (b) Approximate (hoeRL = 0.05 < 0.1 ✓). Ai = −50, Ri = 1100 Ω, Av = −50 × 2000/1100 = −90.9. Error in Ai = (50 − 47.6)/47.6 = 5%.
Check E5. (a) Why are they called hybrid parameters? (b) Which h-parameter is closest to β? (c) For hie = 1 kΩ, hfe = 100, RL = 1 kΩ, use the approximate model to find Ai, Ri and Av. (d) What condition allows the approximate model?
Unit 5 › Amplifier analysis (taught on the slides)

E6 · Multistage amplifiers and the Darlington pair

Practice · deck "Multi-Stage Amplifier" Two amplifier stages with voltage gains 40 and 60 are cascaded. Find the overall gain as a number and in dB.
Guess first: do the gains add or multiply?

Cascading. When one stage cannot give enough gain, the output of one stage feeds the input of the next. The overall gain is the product of the stage gains, where each stage's gain is found with the next stage connected as its load (the input resistance of stage 2 loads stage 1). In decibels, Av(dB) = 20 log10|Av|, and the stage values add.

CouplingHowFor · against
RC couplinga capacitor between stagescheap, small, good in the audio range; the capacitor blocks DC so each stage is biased separately. Gain falls at low frequency.
Transformer couplinga transformer between stagesmatches impedances, so maximum power transfer; bulky, costly, poor frequency response.
Direct couplinga wireamplifies down to DC; the bias of one stage disturbs the next, and drift is amplified.

Darlington pair. The emitter current of Q1 is the base current of Q2, and the collectors are joined. The pair behaves as one "super-β" transistor.

IE1 = (1 + β1)IB, and IE2 = (1 + β2)IE1 = (1 + β1)(1 + β2)IB, so

βD = β1β2 + β1 + β2 ≈ β1β2

Two base–emitter drops in series: VBE ≈ 1.4 V. Very high input resistance. Used as an emitter follower to drive heavy loads. DC bias with RB and RE: IB = (VCC − VBE)/(RB + βDRE).

Answer. Av = 40 × 60 = 2400. In dB: 20 log 40 + 20 log 60 = 32.0 + 35.6 = 67.6 dB (= 20 log 2400).
Check E6. (a) Two transistors with β = 100 each form a Darlington pair. Find βD exactly. (b) Why is the gain of stage 1 lower once stage 2 is connected? (c) Which coupling can amplify a DC signal?

E7 · BJT compared with MOSFET

Input resistancelow to medium (about 1 kΩ in CE); draws input currentextremely high (10¹⁰ Ω and above); draws no DC input current
Transfer lawexponential: IC ∝ eVBE/VTsquare law: ID = K(VGS − VT)²
Transconductancehigh: gm = IC/VT (38 mS at 1 mA)lower at the same current: gm = 2√(K·ID)
Voltage gain per stagehigherlower
TemperatureIC rises with temperature: risk of thermal runawayID falls with temperature (mobility drops): self-limiting
Switchingslowed by stored minority charge in saturationno stored minority charge; limited by gate capacitance
Power in logicdraws base current continuouslyCMOS draws almost nothing when not switching
Size · densitylarger; fewer per chipvery small, simpler to fabricate: millions to billions per chip
Noisemoreless
Handlingrobustgate oxide is damaged by static charge
Best athigh-gain, high-frequency analog and discrete amplifiersdigital ICs, switches, high-input-impedance stages
Check E7. (a) Give two reasons MOSFETs replaced BJTs in digital ICs. (b) Which device gives more voltage gain per stage, and which parameter explains it? (c) Why is a MOSFET thermally more stable?

Answers: Part E Checks

  1. E1. (a) Emitter–base forward, collector–base reverse. (b) IC = IE − IB = 5 − 0.05 = 4.95 mA. (c) Cutoff (open) and saturation (closed).
  2. E2. (a) β = 0.98/0.02 = 49; γ = 50. (b) β = IC/IB = IC/(IE − IC); divide top and bottom by IE: β = α/(1 − α). (c) Common collector (emitter follower): high input resistance, very low output resistance, so it can drive a low-resistance load without loading the stage before it.
  3. E3. (a) IB is unchanged at 47.08 μA, so βIB = 4.71 mA and VCE = 12 − 4.71 × 2.2 = 1.64 V. The Q-point has moved most of the way to saturation, only because β changed: fixed bias is not stable. (b) (VCE, IC) = (12 V, 0) and (0, 3 mA).
  4. E4. (a) IB does not depend on IC, so dIB/dIC = 0 and S = (1 + β)/1. (b) RTh/RE = 10: S = 51 × 11/(51 + 10) = 9.2. (c) ICO doubles per 10 °C; VBE falls about 2.5 mV/°C; β rises. All three increase IC.
  5. E5. (a) Their units differ: an impedance, an admittance and two pure ratios. (b) hfe. (c) Ai = −100, Ri = 1 kΩ, Av = −100 × 1 k/1 k = −100. (d) hoeRL < 0.1.
  6. E6. (a) 100 × 100 + 100 + 100 = 10 200. (b) The input resistance of stage 2 appears in parallel with stage 1's collector resistor, lowering its effective load. (c) Direct coupling.
  7. E7. (a) Almost zero static power in CMOS, and much smaller size, so far higher density (also simpler fabrication). (b) The BJT; its transconductance gm = IC/VT is higher at the same current. (c) Its current falls as temperature rises, because mobility falls, so a hot spot carries less current instead of more.
